A Branch of Theological Psychology

A Discipline Born at the Intersection of Faith, Science and the Human Body.

Introducing Theological Somatics™ — a branch of theological psychology that studies healing through the integration of trauma science, nervous system regulation, spiritual formation and embodied faith.

The Discipline

What is Theological Somatics™?

Theological Somatics™ is the study and practice of healing the fear of hope through the integration of trauma science, nervous system regulation, spiritual formation and embodied faith.

As a branch of theological psychology, it moves beyond cognitive belief into the body — recognizing that healing is not complete until truth is not only understood but felt, regulated and embodied.

For many, faith and nervous system function are not separate systems. They are woven together — and must be healed together.

Theological Somatics™ is original intellectual property founded by Kenya Young.

It is a developing discipline — one that brings language, structure and clinical clarity to experiences long misinterpreted as lack of faith, lack of discipline or personal failure.

Formal Definition

Theological Somatics™ is the study and practice of healing the fear of hope through the integration of trauma science, nervous system regulation, spiritual formation and embodied faith.

Hope Anxiety™, as explored throughout When Hope Feels Dangerous, is a human experience — a nervous system pattern shaped by lived experience, loss, disappointment and the body’s attempt to protect itself from further harm. It can be understood and addressed through multiple lenses, including psychological, behavioral and physiological frameworks.

Theological Somatics™ represents one such lens.

While related to concepts such as somatic theology, Theological Somatics™ centers the nervous system and embodied healing as the primary entry point — integrating faith as part of the healing process rather than the starting framework.

It offers an integrated approach for those who understand their story through both psychology and faith. It creates space for a form of healing that honors both the body’s protective responses and the spiritual formation that shapes how individuals interpret pain, hope and restoration.

Situated at the intersection of two bodies of knowledge that have historically existed in tension — the church and the therapy room — Theological Somatics™ offers the body of Christ a clinical language for suffering beyond “just have faith,” while offering the field of psychology a framework that acknowledges the role of spiritual belief in how many people are wired, wounded and healed.

When Hope Feels Dangerous serves as a foundational text within this emerging area of study — introducing a structured framework for understanding and healing Hope Anxiety™ through both clinical insight and spiritual integration.

The Founding Observation

This discipline was founded on an observation that could not be ignored.

Many people deeply believe in what God can do. They pray. They trust. They hold on to faith.

And yet —

Their bodies still brace. Their nervous systems still activate. Their patterns still interrupt forward movement.

Theological Somatics™ exists to name and understand that disconnect.

It does not replace faith.
It reveals how faith is experienced in the body.

Situated at the intersection of two bodies of knowledge that have historically existed in tension — the church and the therapy room — Theological Somatics™ offers the body of Christ a clinical language for suffering beyond “just have faith,” while offering the field of psychology a framework that acknowledges the role of spiritual belief in how many people are wired, wounded and healed.

The Discipline to Date

Theological Somatics™ has currently identified 8 patterns that reflect how individuals subconsciously resist what their faith promises them. Hope Anxiety™ is the first and most fully developed. The remaining seven have been named and are actively being developed into a fuller body of work.

The First Fully Developed Pattern

Hope Anxiety™

Within this discipline, specific patterns are identified that reflect how individuals subconsciously resist the very things their faith promises them.

Hope Anxiety™ is the first and most fully developed of these patterns — a trauma-rooted nervous system response that activates specifically when something positive is happening, about to happen or could happen — after repeated disappointment, loss or shattered expectations.

Its core mechanism is Forward Motion Disruption — the body’s learned response of bracing, withdrawing or self-sabotaging at the very threshold of breakthrough.

Hope Anxiety™ is a universal human pattern — not limited to any faith tradition. Theological Somatics™ is one specialized lens for addressing it, rooted in the integration of faith and nervous system healing.

Hope Anxiety™ is the subject of Kenya Young’s book — When Hope Feels Dangerous — and the foundation of the HAS-10, a companion clinical-grade assessment tool.

“This is not a redefinition of hope.
It is a reconditioning of how the body learns to experience it.”

Emerging Patterns Within the Discipline

Named. Understood. In Development.

Beyond Hope Anxiety™, Theological Somatics™ identifies additional patterns that reflect how the body resists what the spirit desires. These patterns have been named and are currently being developed into a fuller body of work.

Receiving Resistance™
The inability to receive good things — love, praise, provision — without deflecting or minimizing.
Joy Suspicion™
Distrust of joy itself, as though happiness is a precursor to loss.
Peace Intolerance™
Discomfort with calm seasons, often creating chaos to return to a familiar state.
Provision Panic™
Anxiety that activates around financial increase, abundance or unexpected blessing.
Calling Avoidance™
Subconscious resistance to stepping fully into purpose, often disguised as humility or waiting.
Grace Friction™
Difficulty accepting grace without earning it — rooted in performance-based worth.
Expectation Collapse™
The preemptive lowering of expectations to protect against disappointment before it happens.

Here, those patterns are named.
Here, they are understood.
And here, they can begin to change.

A Developing Discipline

As a developing discipline, Theological Somatics™ continues to expand — bringing language, structure and clinical clarity to experiences long misinterpreted as lack of faith, lack of discipline or personal failure.

This is not a redefinition of hope.
It is a reconditioning of how the body learns to experience it.
